method: Questions were researched with an evidence-only retrieval tool over one corpus of open-access and public-domain texts (see corpus.json). Each excerpt was checked word for word against the corpus passage it cites when this file was written; corpus_chunk numbers that passage in the corpus snapshot of 2026-10-01.
questions: How did Socrates, Plato and Aristotle distinguish knowledge from true belief?
What are the three definitions of knowledge in the Theaetetus, and why do they fail?
How did Aristotle answer the regress argument against scientific knowledge?
How did the Stoics and the Academic skeptics argue about the cognitive impression?
Did the Pyrrhonists hold that nothing can be known?

Theaetetus proposes a second definition of knowledge: (D2) “Knowledge is true belief (orthê doxa).”
He dismisses D2 just by arguing that accidental true beliefs cannot be called knowledge, giving Athenian jurymen as an example of accidental true belief.
A skilled lawyer can bring jurymen into a state of true belief without bringing them into a state of knowledge; so knowledge and true belief are different states.
The jury argument seems to be a counter-example not only to D2 but also to D3

Plato seems to offer two incompatible explanations of why the jury don’t know: first that they have only a limited time to hear the arguments (201b3, 172e1); and second that their judgement is second-hand (201b9)

One crucial question about Theaetetus 201–210 is the question whether the argument is concerned with objectual or propositional knowledge. This is a basic and central division among interpretations of the whole
Whatever is scientifically known must be demonstrated.
Either this process continues forever, creating an infinite regress of premises, or it comes to a stop at some point.
If it continues forever, then there are no first premises from which the subsequent ones are demonstrated, and so nothing is demonstrated.
On the other hand, if it comes to a stop at some point, then the premises at which it comes to a stop are undemonstrated and therefore not scientifically known

circular demonstration gives us a regress that is both unending (in the sense that we never reach premises at which it comes to a stop) and finite (because it works its way round the finite circle of premises)
